author: ChatGPT
title: The Alignment Lab — Discover eigenvectors
notice: CHATGPT-AUTHORED DRAFT — requires implementation and educational play review. Not yet an approved lesson.
objectives: Distinguish a matrix changing an arrow's direction from merely changing its length or reversing it.
Predict a concrete 2×2 matrix output before seeing the result, then connect it to direction.
Discover a non-zero eigendirection by active manipulation and verify it numerically.
Compute A v by row-by-vector multiplication; test whether A v = λ v using one scalar for both coordinates.
Identify a negative eigenvalue as reversal along the same line and recognise non-axis eigendirections.
Transfer the test to an unseen matrix without visual assistance.
successCriteria: In challenge 1, the learner commits an output prediction before the correct output is revealed, with authored feedback for each choice.
In challenge 3, the learner actively finds and locks a non-zero horizontal vector for shear matrix [[1,1],[0,1]]; merely moving controls does not mark success.
In challenge 4, the learner calculates the hidden output (3,1) for input (2,1) with no result readout until correct.
In challenge 5, the learner identifies that (-2,0) stays on the same line as (1,0) and correctly supplies multiplier -2.
In challenge 6, the learner identifies both candidate eigendirections of [[2,1],[1,2]] and supplies eigenvalues 3 and 1 without early result reveal.

In challenge 7, the learner answers two transfer questions with diagrams hidden; the UI records number of attempts and use of hints, so a first-try no-hint pass can be distinguished from coached completion.
Every learner-facing message, accessible description, feedback, visual label, hint, action and progression condition comes from this specification; no implementer-authored teaching.
The experience is evaluated with a real learner for clarity, sustained attention and independent calculation; green tests alone are insufficient.

steps.title: The Alignment Lab
body: A matrix is a rule that takes one arrow and produces another. Usually, the new arrow points somewhere different.
But certain directions are special. A matrix can stretch an arrow, shrink it, or even reverse it without moving it off its original straight line.

Your challenge: find those directions, explain why they work, and prove it with numbers. You'll make predictions before the result appears. Guessing is allowed; the important part is understanding what changes.
Seven short challenges. First you'll see what the machine does. By the end, the diagram disappears.

steps.title: 1 / Predict the machine
body: The teal arrow starts at (2, 1). The matrix doubles x and leaves y unchanged.
Before the orange result appears, choose where you think its tip will land.

copy.graphDescription: A teal arrow runs from (0, 0) to (2, 1). The orange result is hidden until the correct prediction is committed. After success, it extends to (4, 1); a full straight-line guide through the original arrow makes the turn visible.
copy.hintText: Read the rows: the new x is 2 × 2 + 0 × 1. The new y is 0 × 2 + 1 × 1.
copy.question: Where will the orange arrow end?
copy.feedbackA: Correct. x goes from 2 to 4, while y stays 1. The result is (4, 1). Watch how the arrow changes direction.
copy.feedbackB: That would leave both coordinates unchanged. But this matrix doubles the x coordinate.
copy.feedbackC: That doubles both coordinates. Check the bottom row of the matrix: it leaves y unchanged.
copy.feedbackD: You have changed the wrong coordinates. The x coordinate doubles; y stays the same.
copy.revealExplanation: Notice that (4, 1) is not twice (2, 1). If it were twice, the result would be (4, 2). The arrow has turned.
copy.a11yChoices: Choose one of four possible endpoint coordinates. The transformed arrow is hidden until you commit a correct answer.
copy.a11yReveal: The input is (2, 1). The output is (4, 1). They do not lie on the same straight line through the origin.

steps.title: 2 / Same line or different line?
body: Both arrows are visible now. Imagine extending the teal arrow into an infinite straight line through (0, 0).
Would the orange arrow sit on that same line?

copy.graphDescription: The teal arrow goes to (2, 1). The orange arrow goes to (4, 1). An infinite line continues the teal arrow through the origin. The orange endpoint is off that line.
copy.hintText: If the result were on the teal line, both coordinates would have to be multiplied by the same number.
copy.question: Which statement is true?
copy.feedbackA: Not this time. Doubling the x coordinate but not the y coordinate changes the angle.
copy.feedbackB: Correct. The result is off the teal line, so this is not a special direction for this matrix.
copy.feedbackC: The arrows do not even have the same endpoint: one ends at (2, 1), the other at (4, 1).
copy.revealExplanation: To stay on the same line, the output must equal one number times the ENTIRE input vector. One multiplier must work for both coordinates.
copy.a11yChoices: Choose whether the input and result lie on the same straight line through the origin.
copy.a11yReveal: (4, 1) cannot be written as a single multiple of (2, 1). The first coordinate needs multiplier 2 and the second needs multiplier 1.

steps.title: 3 / Find the safe heading
body: A new matrix is active. This one adds y to x, but leaves y alone.
Move the teal arrow. Your goal is to make the orange result stay on the teal arrow's straight line. Both arrows must be non-zero.
When you find a direction that works, lock it in.

copy.graphDescription: The teal arrow is movable on integer grid points from -3 to 3 in each coordinate. Its output is (x + y, y). The orange arrow updates live. A straight guide extends the teal direction in both directions; aligned arrows lie on that guide. The origin alone does not qualify.
copy.hintText: Try setting y to zero. What does adding y to x do then?
copy.question: Can you find a non-zero direction the machine does not turn?
copy.feedbackZero: (0, 0) has no direction. Move the teal tip away from the origin.
copy.feedbackTurned: The orange arrow still leaves the teal line. Compare what happens when you change y.
copy.feedbackCorrect: You found one. With y = 0, the machine adds zero to x. The result stays on the same straight line.
copy.revealExplanation: For this matrix, every non-zero horizontal arrow keeps its direction and its length. For example, (2, 0) becomes (2, 0). A slanted arrow usually turns.
copy.a11yChoices: Drag the teal vector tip or use the two coordinate controls. Only whole-number coordinates from -3 to 3 are available. Press Lock this heading to test the selected vector.
copy.a11yReveal: The correct directions are the non-zero horizontal vectors. Their y coordinate is zero.

steps.title: 4 / Do the calculation
body: Keep the same matrix, but start with (2, 1). This time the orange arrow stays hidden until you've calculated it.
Multiply each row of the matrix by the input vector. Enter the two coordinates you get.

copy.graphDescription: A teal arrow from (0, 0) to (2, 1) is shown. The orange result is hidden until both numeric coordinates are entered correctly. The matrix is [[1, 1], [0, 1]]. The result is (3, 1).
copy.question: What is A × (2, 1)?
copy.feedbackInvalid: Enter a number in each box. Use numerals, not expressions.
copy.feedbackXOnly: Your x coordinate is correct. For y, use the bottom row: 0 × 2 + 1 × 1.
copy.feedbackYOnly: Your y coordinate is correct. For x, use the top row: 1 × 2 + 1 × 1.
copy.feedbackNeither: Calculate the rows separately. Each row gives one output coordinate.
copy.feedbackCorrect: Correct: (3, 1). Now compare it with (2, 1): the arrow has turned.
copy.revealExplanation: Top row: 1 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 3. Bottom row: 0 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 1. So A × (2, 1) = (3, 1). This is not one number times (2, 1), so (2, 1) is not an eigendirection.
copy.a11yChoices: Enter the two output coordinates. The output arrow is hidden until the calculation is correct.
copy.a11yReveal: The original vector (2, 1) becomes (3, 1). Since the coordinate ratios differ, the vector changes direction.

steps.title: 5 / Backwards still counts
body: This machine turns (1, 0) into (−2, 0). The orange arrow points backwards.
First decide whether it stays on the same straight line. Then give the single number that multiplies (1, 0) to make (−2, 0).

copy.graphDescription: The teal arrow points right from (0, 0) to (1, 0). The orange arrow points left from (0, 0) to (-2, 0). Both occupy the same horizontal straight line through the origin, but face opposite ways.
copy.hintText: A negative multiplier reverses an arrow. Compare −2 × (1, 0) with the orange arrow.
copy.lineQuestion: Are both arrows on the same straight line?
copy.scaleQuestion: What number multiplies the teal arrow to get the orange arrow?
copy.feedbackInvalid: Choose Yes or No, and enter a number for the multiplier.
copy.feedbackWrongLine: They point in opposite directions, but they still lie on the same horizontal line. Try again.
copy.feedbackPositiveScale: A multiplier of +2 would point right. The result points left.
copy.feedbackWrongScale: Use the x coordinates: result x ÷ input x = −2 ÷ 1.
copy.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The arrow is reversed and twice as long, but it is still on the same line. The multiplier is −2.
copy.revealExplanation: A vector that stays on its original line under a matrix is an eigenvector, as long as it is not (0, 0). The number multiplying it is its eigenvalue. Here, (1, 0) is an eigenvector and −2 is its eigenvalue. Negative does not mean 'wrong direction'; it means reversed.
copy.a11yChoices: Choose whether the arrows are on the same line, then type the multiplier. The orange result is (-2, 0).
copy.a11yReveal: The result is -2 times the input. The eigenvalue is -2.

steps.title: 6 / Two hidden corridors
body: One matrix can have more than one direction that survives. This machine mixes x and y.
Four candidate directions are shown. Find the TWO that stay on their original lines, then calculate the multiplier for each. You can use the matrix to work it out before choosing.
Choose two different candidates and enter their multipliers. The result arrows stay hidden until you solve the pair.

copy.graphDescription: Four candidate teal arrows are displayed on separate equal-scale grids. A is (1, 1), B is (1, -1), C is (2, 1), and D is (1, 0). Their output arrows are hidden until the solution is checked. The matrix is [[2, 1], [1, 2]].
copy.hintText: Try A first. (2 × 1 + 1 × 1, 1 × 1 + 2 × 1) = (3, 3). Is that a multiple of (1, 1)? Then check B.
copy.question: Which TWO directions survive, and what is each multiplier?
copy.feedbackInvalid: Select exactly two different candidates and enter one numeric multiplier for each.
copy.feedbackContainsC: C becomes (5, 4). To stay on the same line as (2, 1), both coordinates would need the same multiplier. They don't.
copy.feedbackContainsD: D becomes (2, 1). It started horizontal but now has y = 1, so it turns.
copy.feedbackWrongScaleA: A becomes (3, 3), which is 3 × (1, 1). Check its multiplier.
copy.feedbackWrongScaleB: B becomes (1, −1), which is 1 × (1, −1). Check its multiplier.
copy.feedbackCorrect: Both found. A stretches three times along the diagonal. B keeps exactly the same length along the other diagonal.
copy.revealExplanation: For A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], the direction (1, 1) has eigenvalue 3, and (1, −1) has eigenvalue 1. These special directions are not limited to horizontal or vertical arrows.
copy.a11yChoices: Choose two candidate vectors from A, B, C and D. Enter a multiplier for each selected vector. Each candidate is shown on its own grid; no result vectors are revealed before success.
copy.a11yReveal: Candidate A (1, 1) becomes (3, 3) with eigenvalue 3. Candidate B (1, -1) becomes (1, -1) with eigenvalue 1.

steps.title: 7 / No diagram. Your turn.
body: The final test has no picture until you've answered. You have the matrix and two vectors.
Part A: calculate the output for (2, 0) and give its multiplier. Part B: decide whether (1, 1) is an eigenvector of the same matrix.
Take your time. The point is to use the reasoning, not remember a picture.

copy.graphDescription: No diagram is visible before a correct final answer. When revealed, the matrix [[3, 0], [0, 2]] sends (2, 0) to (6, 0), staying horizontal; it sends (1, 1) to (3, 2), which leaves the diagonal.
copy.hintText: Multiply each row by the vector. An eigenvector requires ONE multiplier that works for both coordinates.
copy.partAQuestion: Part A — If the input is (2, 0), what is the output?
copy.partAScaleQuestion: Part A — What is the eigenvalue?
copy.partBQuestion: Part B — Is (1, 1) an eigenvector of this matrix?
copy.feedbackInvalid: Complete both coordinate fields, the eigenvalue field and the Yes/No decision.
copy.feedbackWrongOutput: For Part A, the first row gives 3 × 2 + 0 × 0, and the second gives 0 × 2 + 2 × 0.
copy.feedbackWrongScale: For Part A, compare the output (6, 0) with the input (2, 0). What number multiplies the whole vector?
copy.feedbackWrongClassification: For Part B, (1, 1) becomes (3, 2). One coordinate is tripled, the other doubled. Can one multiplier do both?
copy.feedbackCorrect: You did it without the diagram. For Part A, (2, 0) becomes (6, 0) with eigenvalue 3. For Part B, (1, 1) is not an eigenvector because it becomes (3, 2).
copy.revealExplanation: The rule is A v = λ v for a non-zero vector v. In ordinary language: apply the matrix, and the result must be one number times the entire original vector. Stretching, shrinking, staying unchanged and reversing can all count. Turning does not.
copy.a11yChoices: Complete three numeric fields for Part A and a Yes/No choice for Part B. The diagram is withheld until the whole answer is correct.
copy.a11yReveal: With matrix [[3, 0], [0, 2]], (2, 0) maps to (6, 0), lambda 3. Vector (1, 1) maps to (3, 2) and is not an eigenvector.

steps.title: Alignment achieved
body: You now have a test you can use on any matrix and non-zero vector: calculate A v, then ask whether one number λ multiplies the whole original vector to give that result.
If one number works, the vector is an eigenvector and that number is its eigenvalue. If the output turns off the original straight line, it is not.
This run checks what you can do today. It does not prove you'll remember tomorrow. Come back later and try the final challenge without hints or looking at the earlier stages.
